To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Bolivia’s forest sector has been characterized by a constant change in regulations that were intended to improve the legality in the forest and land use sector and the forest sector in general.

Bolivia’s forest regulations and policies have undergone many modifications in the last two decades, but the new regulations and policy changes were not sufficient to address the new and often illegal practices that emerged as a result of the reforms.
Bolivia’s domestic timber value chain operates with a mix of legally allowable and informally practicable practices.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what is legally allowed and what is informally practicable.

the question of how the Bolivian state and the Bolivian forest sector responded to new illegal practices in the forest sector that emerged as a result of the new forest regulations, and how these responses affected legality.
the question of what the legally allowed versus the informally practical in Bolivia’s domestic forest sector and timber market are, and why.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new forest regulations have not been effective in reducing illegal logging in Bolivia.
Bolivia has not yet been able to establish a legal timber market, but it has made some progress in the right direction.
the new forest regulatory and forest policies have been inadequate to ensure the legal production and trade of timber and related forest products in Bolivia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the legally allowable and the informally practicables in Bolivia’s domestic forestry sector have changed considerably in the past two decades, and the latter have often been more successful than the former.
the Bolivian forest sector is in a constant process of change, with new regulations and policies being developed and modified, and new actors entering the sector.
the new forest regulatory framework in Bolivia was not adequate and that the implementation and enforcement of the new regulations was poor and that this led to new illegalities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the legal framework is not necessarily an accurate reflection of what is practicable.

the Bolivian forest sector is a good example of the need for a new forest law and policy that addresses the new illegal practices that have emerged in the last two decades and that are likely to continue to emerge in the near future.
legality is not a fixed concept, but a moving target that is influenced and shaped by a wide range of factors.
